This means you need to carefully consider and document the equality impact of processing personal data where it can be used to identify individuals as having a protected characteristic. This document is often referred to as an Equality Impact Assessment (EIA). For more information, consult the EHRC guidance on the Public Sector Equality Duty.

You must comply with equality legislation at all times, including:

The Public Sector Equality Duty requires that you show ‘due regard’ for the aims of the duty fulfilled before, and at the time that a particular policy or operational activity that will or might impact people with protected characteristics is under consideration, as well as at the time a decision is taken. Assessing impact is an integral part of this duty, and the completion of an Equality Impact Assessment (EIA) is an effective means of fulfilling this.

Field text:
Before you begin building a tool or system, you should develop a plan to monitor and evaluate the environmental impact. There are various environmental factors that you should monitor and manage across the lifecycle of your project. This can be a complex task but it’s vital for ensuring proper stewardship of data and AI projects. 
 
You should select appropriate metrics and key performance indicators (KPIs) that can be tracked over time – such as carbon footprint, energy consumption or compute efficiency. You may need to consider more than one metric to understand the project’s broader impact.

The sustainability chapter in the Data and AI Ethics Framework provides further guidance on how to do this.  

The Service Manual has guidance on how to build more environmentally sustainable digital services in government.
Hint text: It’s important to consider environmental sustainability and impact from the start of your project, as it can influence your choices about tools, suppliers and infrastructure.

Field text: Is your tool within scope of the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS)?
Context filter: FILTER=data OR ai OR personal OR public OR decision OR critical

Field text:
The ATRS establishes a standardised way for public sector organisations to publish information about how and why they are using algorithmic tools. The ATRS is mandatory for: 				
• All government departments, and for ALBs which deliver public or frontline services, or directly interact with the general public.				
• Algorithmic tools which have a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect or directly interact with the general public.				
				
If your organisation and tools fall within the mandatory scope of the ATRS, you are required to complete and openly publish an ATRS record once your project reaches public beta.				
				
The ATRS template, guidance for completing a record, and the repository of published records are all hosted on the ATRS Hub on GOV.UK. You can reach the ATRS team at algorithmic-transparency@dsit.gov.uk.

You should check if your tool is in scope of the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS). 

The ATRS is mandatory for: 
•	All government departments, and for ALBs which deliver public or frontline services, or directly interact with the general public.
•	Algorithmic tools which have a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect or directly interact with the general public.

The mandatory requirement to publish an ATRS record applies to tools that are in Beta/Pilot or Production phase.
It is recommended best practice to publish an ATRS record even if your tool is not within mandatory scope.

Field text: How are you notifying users that they are using or interacting with an AI system rather than a human?
Context filter: FILTER=data OR ai OR personal OR public OR decision OR critical
Hint text:
You should consider how different groups, particularly groups such as children, the elderly and vulnerable persons, can recognise and identify whether they are interacting with an AI system or a human. 

Systems for notification may include explicit opening statements and persistent labels (for example, stating that the system is ‘powered by AI’), distinct visual cues such as robotic icons, or watermarking on AI-generated text, and reminders in conversation flows. Consider how effective these notifications are in practice for different user groups and in different situations.
